read: full: pages 1-12 (abstract, introduction, methods, experimental settings, results, cost, conclusions and limitations, appendix A.1-A.3 with Tables 4-8); the judge-prompt tables on pages 12-17 skimmed
venue_now: arXiv 2404.18796v2, 1 May 2024 (p.1 footer); this text shows no venue; papers.json records arXiv only as of 2026-10
what_it_is: A study of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation that proposes a Panel of LLm evaluators (PoLL): several judges from different model families score each output independently and their verdicts are pooled, by max voting for binary QA correctness and by averaging for 1-5 scores (p.2-3). The panel instantiated is Command R, Claude 3 Haiku and GPT-3.5 (p.3). Across single-hop QA (KILT NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA), multi-hop QA (Bamboogle, HotpotQA) and Chatbot Arena Hard, judges are compared with human correctness labels (Cohen's kappa) and with Arena Elo rankings (Pearson, Kendall tau) (p.3-4). The panel agrees with humans more closely than a single GPT-4 judge, shows less intra-model bias and costs seven to eight times less (p.1, p.4-6).
domain: LLM-as-a-judge for open-domain, retrieval-augmented question answering (single- and multi-hop) and for chatbot response preference
size: 3 settings, 6 datasets (p.2-3); Arena Hard has 500 prompts (p.3) and Bamboogle 125 questions (p.10). Human labels: NQ 688 examples (triple-annotated), TriviaQA 316 (single), HotpotQA single-hop 784 (triple), HotpotQA multi-hop 595 (single), Bamboogle 750 (single) (Table 8, p.12). Judges: Command R, Haiku, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and the three-model panel; evaluated models include Command R and R+, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, Claude 3 Haiku and Sonnet, Mistral Large and Medium (p.3).
source_of_items: existing QA datasets and Arena Hard prompts; answers generated by the evaluated models; human correctness labels collected for the study (p.3-4, p.11)
has_gold_traces: no (reference answers only; the judged outputs are QA answers and chat responses)
evaluation: LLM judge, single or panel, validated against human labels: reference-based binary correctness for QA (Cohen's kappa) and pairwise preference for Arena Hard (rank correlation with Arena Elo) (p.2-4)
human_validation: Professional annotators from Cohere's internal workforce (novelists, copywriters, copy editors, journalists) judged whether the reference answer is semantically contained in each generated answer (p.4, p.11). NQ and single-hop HotpotQA were triple-annotated and pooled by majority vote; the other sets were singly annotated (p.11, Table 8 p.12). No inter-annotator agreement is reported. Chatbot Arena crowd Elo serves as ground truth for the ranking setting (p.3-4).
contamination_measures: none (not applicable to a judge study)

engtrace_use.sentence: Building upon the 'Panel of LLM' (PoLL) methodology (Verga et al., 2024), we construct an 'AI Tribunal' comprising three frontier reasoning models: GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025a), Claude Opus 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025b), and Gemini 3 (Google, 2025). (sec. 3.3, May L260-266)
engtrace_use.explanation: What the Tribunal takes from PoLL is right: several judges from different model families scoring independently, with their verdicts pooled (p.2-3). Three things are loose. (1) PoLL's premise is a panel of smaller models replacing a single large one ('very large models are often unnecessary', p.1), and its advantages are lower cost and less intra-model bias (p.1, p.6); a tribunal of three frontier models inverts the size and cost argument and keeps only the family-diversity one. (2) PoLL's evidence covers reference-based QA correctness and chatbot preference (p.2-4); its authors say further work is needed to see whether it applies to 'math or reasoning evaluations' (p.6), and auditing template code and instances against a multi-axis rubric lies further still from what was tested. (3) The aggregation differs: PoLL uses max voting or average pooling (p.3), the Tribunal a median threshold, a majority veto and a disagreement score (May L270-300). Also, PoLL stands for 'Panel of LLm evaluators' (p.1), not 'Panel of LLM'. 'Building upon' is a fair statement of inspiration, but the sentence implies more support than the paper gives.

suggested_wording: Single LLM judges tend to favour their own outputs, and a panel of three judges from disjoint model families agreed with human correctness labels on open-domain QA more closely than GPT-4 alone (Verga et al., 2024); the template screen accordingly uses three judges from three families, none of them on the evaluated roster.
facts_to_cite: PoLL: each judge scores an output independently and the scores are pooled by a voting function, max voting for binary QA correctness and average pooling for 1-5 Arena scores (p.2-3).
The panel was Command R, Claude 3 Haiku and GPT-3.5, drawn from three disjoint model families (p.3).

Cohen's kappa with human correctness labels, panel against a single GPT-4 judge: 0.763 vs 0.627 on NQ, 0.906 vs 0.841 on TriviaQA, 0.867 vs 0.830 on HotpotQA; Haiku alone reached 0.873 on HotpotQA (Table 1, p.4).
Against the Chatbot Arena ranking, the panel reached Pearson 0.917 and Kendall tau 0.778, GPT-4 0.817 and 0.667 (Table 2, p.4).
GPT-4's kappa on NQ ranged from 0.518 (zero-shot) to 0.725 ('don't overthink' prompt) across prompt variants (Table 3, p.5).

Intra-model bias: on Bamboogle each judged model's largest positive deviation from the human score occurred when it judged itself (p.5, Figure 4 p.6); the GPT-4 judge placed a GPT-4 variant 2nd on Arena Hard against its 4th place in the Arena ranking (p.5).
The three-model panel cost seven to eight times less than a single GPT-4 Turbo judge (p.6).
The authors call for further work on whether the method applies to math or reasoning evaluations, and leave panel selection to future work (p.6).
Human labels: professional annotators judged whether the reference answer is contained in the generated answer; two datasets triple-annotated, three singly (p.4, p.11, Table 8 p.12).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: validating a judge against human labels with an agreement coefficient, using judges from different families, and concern with self-preference, which EngTrace's roster rule addresses (no judge model on the roster, D-110) and its judge-overlap check measures (pooled score 0.379 with suite judges vs 0.378 with non-suite judges, state brief sec. 3). Lacks: reasoning or step-level judging (it judges final QA answers and chat responses, p.2-4), mathematics or engineering, generated instances, gold traces and expert raters (its annotators are writers and editors, p.11, with no agreement statistic). In one respect EngTrace's current evaluator runs against PoLL's recommendation: its residual judge is a single model (MiMo-V2.5-Pro), justified by expert validation (E5 milestone F1 0.958 against 15 experts in X1, state brief sec. 3) and family separation from the roster, not by pooling.
notes: Batch V question: in the planned judge-validity paragraph PoLL is a citation for (a) self-preference and intra-model bias in single judges (p.2, p.5), (b) agreement with human labels as the test of a judge (p.4), and (c) the prompt sensitivity of a strong judge (p.5). Now that the AI Tribunal is only the Layer 1 template screen, with three judges from outside the roster (Grok 4.6, MiniMax M3, MiMo-V2.5-Pro, state brief sec. 1), the revised text may say the screen follows PoLL in drawing its judges from different families. It should not say the screen uses smaller models, nor cite PoLL as validating code or rubric audits. It must not cite PoLL in support of the single residual judge; better to acknowledge PoLL's case against single judges and answer it with the expert validation and the separation from the roster. Keep the self-preference evidence modest: one dataset's figure and one ranking (p.5). The panel's edge also depends on the prompt: with the prompt optimised for GPT-4, the panel's NQ kappa falls to 0.699, below GPT-4's 0.725 and Haiku's 0.757 (Table 4, p.10), and on multi-hop HotpotQA Command R (0.886) beats the panel (0.871) (Table 6, p.11). If the appendix keeps the pilot's three-judge E0 panel (E0-3J, state brief sec. 3), that is the other place PoLL fits.
